title: OST2 Arch1001 02: Registers, First Instruction (NOP) and the Stack

questions.q: In the computer memory hierarchy, what sits at the very top: the smallest capacity and the fastest access?
questions.explain: Registers are built into the processor. There are only tens to hundreds of bytes of them, they are the fastest storage, and assembly instructions operate on them directly.

questions.q: Which of these lose their contents when the system is powered off (volatile memory)?
questions.explain: Registers, cache and RAM are volatile. Flash, hard drives and tape are non-volatile storage that keeps its contents after power-off.

questions.q: Which ordering goes from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest?
choices: Registers, cache, RAM, flash, hard drives, tape
Cache, registers, RAM, hard drives, flash, tape
Registers, RAM, cache, flash, tape, hard drives
Registers, cache, flash, RAM, hard drives, tape
questions.explain: Registers > cache (MB, very fast) > RAM (GB, fast) > flash (slower, cheap) > hard drives (multiple TB, slow) > tape (can reach petabytes, very slow).

questions.q: Processor cache typically has more capacity than RAM.
questions.explain: Cache is on the order of megabytes and RAM is on the order of gigabytes. Cache is faster, but it is expensive to build into the processor, so there is less of it.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the processor cache?
choices: To keep data after the power is turned off
To make memory accesses faster than going all the way out to RAM
To add extra general purpose registers
questions.explain: The cache sits between registers and RAM so that frequently used data can be reached faster than a full trip to RAM. It is still volatile.

questions.q: How many general purpose registers does x86-64 have?
questions.explain: RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSP, RBP, RSI, RDI plus R8 through R15. The instruction pointer (RIP) is separate and not counted among them.

questions.q: How many general purpose registers did 32-bit x86 have?
questions.explain: EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX, ESP, EBP, ESI, EDI (plus EIP). The 64-bit extension doubled this to 16.

questions.q: Why did the 64-bit extension increase the number of general purpose registers from 8 to 16?
choices: To give compilers more registers in which to juggle values
Because 64-bit registers cannot be split into sub-registers
So each register can hold two separate 32-bit values
questions.explain: More registers let compilers keep more values in fast storage instead of moving them to and from memory.

questions.q: Which processor introduced the 32-bit 'extended' register EAX?
questions.explain: 8008: 8-bit A. 8086: 16-bit AX (A eXtended) with AH/AL. 80386: 32-bit EAX (Extended AX). AMD Opteron / Intel Pentium 4: 64-bit RAX.

questions.q: Which bits of RAX does AH refer to?
questions.explain: AX is bits 15-0. AH (A High) is its upper byte, bits 15-8. AL (A Low) is bits 7-0.

questions.q: Name a register that refers to the low 32 bits of RAX.
questions.explain: EAX, also called R0D (R0 Double word). AX / R0W is the low 16 bits and AL / R0B is the low 8.

questions.q: In the R0-R15 naming scheme, which register is R3?
questions.explain: The numbering is not alphabetical: R0=RAX, R1=RCX, R2=RDX, R3=RBX, R4=RSP, R5=RBP, R6=RSI, R7=RDI. The order comes from history and instruction encoding.

questions.q: What does R10W refer to?
questions.explain: Suffixes follow Intel's size names: D = double word (32 bits), W = word (16 bits), B = byte (8 bits).

questions.q: Which names refer to all or part of the same register as RSP?
questions.explain: RSP = R4. ESP = R4D, SP = R4W, SPL = R4B. RSI is R6, and BPL and R5 belong to RBP.

questions.q: Which of these 8-bit registers could NOT be accessed before AMD's 64-bit extensions?
questions.explain: The low bytes of SP, BP, SI and DI (SPL, BPL, SIL, DIL) were added with the 64-bit extensions for a consistent naming scheme. AL/AH, BL/BH, CL/CH and DL/DH date back to the 16-bit 8086.

questions.q: R8 has a high-byte sub-register (an 'R8H') like AH is for RAX.
questions.explain: R8-R15 expose only their D (32-bit), W (16-bit) and B (low 8-bit) parts. High-byte registers (AH, BH, CH, DH) exist only for the original A-D registers.

questions.q: Most disassemblers display the first general purpose register as r0 rather than rax.
questions.explain: rax and r0 are just two mnemonics for the same register, and the disassembler chooses which to print. Most use the alphabetical names that people know from older architectures.

questions.q: What is the 64-bit instruction pointer register called?
questions.explain: IP (16-bit), EIP (32-bit), RIP (64-bit). It points at the next instruction to execute.

questions.q: In Intel terminology, a 4-byte value is a:
questions.explain: Byte = 1 byte, word = 2, double word = 4, quad word = 8. These are where the B/W/D register suffixes come from.

questions.q: The 'R' in RAX can be read as:
choices: 'Return' AX, because it holds return values
questions.explain: RAX is the 64-bit extension of EAX. The new scheme also calls it R0, so R can mean 'really wide' or just 'register'.

questions.q: Under Intel's convention, which register holds a function's return value?
questions.explain: RAX stores function return values.

questions.q: Which register is conventionally the counter for string and loop operations?
questions.explain: RCX: C for Counter.

questions.q: By convention, RSI and RDI are:
choices: Source and destination index pointers for string operations
The stack pointer and the instruction pointer
The return value register and the loop counter
The I/O pointer and the data-section base pointer
questions.explain: RSI = Source Index, RDI = Destination Index. Both are pointers used in string operations.

questions.q: What does RBP conventionally point to?
choices: The base of the current stack frame
The base of the data section
questions.explain: RBP = stack frame Base Pointer. RSP points at the top of the stack, RIP at the next instruction, and Intel suggests RBX as a base pointer to the data section.

questions.q: What is Intel's suggested use for RDX?
questions.explain: Intel suggests RDX as an I/O pointer.

questions.q: Intel originally suggested that the A register be the ___, where arithmetic results build up (e.g. the result of 1 + 2 goes back into it).
questions.explain: A was the accumulator. Modern compilers don't follow that much, but RAX still holds return values.

questions.q: Because RSI is the 'source index', a compiler may only use it for string operations.
questions.explain: These are only Intel's suggestions. RSI, RDI and the others are general purpose, and the compiler can use them however it wants.

questions.q: Which register points at the next instruction the processor should execute?
questions.explain: RIP is the instruction pointer.

questions.q: What does the NOP instruction do?
choices: Nothing: it takes no operands and changes no registers or values
Halts the processor until an interrupt arrives
Pops the top of the stack and discards it
questions.explain: NOP = No Operation: no registers, no values, nothing happens.

questions.q: What are NOPs used for?
choices: Padding/aligning code, e.g. so functions start on aligned addresses
Delaying time by using up cycles
questions.explain: Compilers insert NOPs for alignment (following Intel's optimization guidance). Some architectures use them to delay time, and attackers use them to make exploits more reliable.

questions.q: What is the canonical single-byte encoding of NOP, in hex?
questions.explain: 0x90 is the canonical one-byte NOP.

questions.q: The one-byte NOP is an alias mnemonic for which instruction?
choices: PUSH EAX followed by POP EAX
questions.explain: XCHG swaps the values of two registers. Exchanging EAX (or RAX) with itself changes nothing, so it acts as a no-op. XOR EAX, EAX would zero the register.

questions.q: Intel specifies NOP forms ranging from 1 byte up to how many bytes long?
questions.explain: 0x90 is the canonical 1-byte form, but Intel defines NOP forms 1 to 9 bytes long.

questions.q: The NOP padding a compiler places between functions normally gets executed as part of the program's flow.
questions.explain: Alignment NOPs between functions are only there to pad bytes so the next function starts on an aligned address. Execution doesn't reach them.

questions.q: In GCC objdump output, after main's final retq you see `nopw %cs:0x0(%rax,%rax,1)` and `xchg %ax,%ax`. What are these most likely to be?
choices: Multi-byte NOP padding that follows the function
Code that restores registers before returning
Part of main's return value calculation
Instructions that zero the stack after main
questions.explain: They come after the ret, so they never run. nopw is a multi-byte NOP and xchg %ax,%ax swaps a register with itself. Both just fill space for alignment.

questions.q: What kind of data structure is the stack?
questions.explain: Data is pushed onto the top and popped off the top, like a stack of plates. You can't take items out of the middle.

questions.q: Where does the stack live?
choices: In an area of main memory (RAM) that the OS designates when the program starts
On disk, in the swap file
questions.explain: The stack is a conceptual area of RAM that the OS assigns to the program when it starts. RSP just points into it.

questions.q: Why might the stack start at a different address on different systems or on different runs?
choices: Different operating systems follow different conventions for where to put it
Address space layout randomization (ASLR) can move it from one run to the next
The CPU picks a new stack address every time an instruction runs
The stack address is set in the C source code
questions.explain: The OS decides where the stack goes. With ASLR, the location can change each time the program is invoked.

questions.q: By convention, which way do the stack and the heap grow?
choices: Stack toward lower addresses, heap toward higher addresses
Stack toward higher addresses, heap toward lower addresses
questions.explain: The stack grows down toward low addresses ('the enemy's plate is down') and the heap grows up, so they grow toward each other.

questions.q: What happens if a program uses too much stack and too much heap?
choices: They grow into each other and collide, and the program hits an error and is terminated
The stack automatically moves to disk
The heap reverses direction to make room
Nothing: the stack and heap are on separate physical chips
questions.explain: The stack grows down and the heap grows up. If both grow too far they collide, and the program errors out and has to be terminated.

questions.q: What does RSP point to?
choices: The top of the stack: the lowest address currently in use
The bottom of the stack: the highest stack address
The first free slot just below the top of the stack
The base of the current function's frame
questions.explain: RSP points at the last value put on the stack, which is the lowest address being used. RBP is the one that points at the frame base.

questions.q: Memory just past the top of the stack (below RSP) can still hold data, but it should be treated as undefined and never relied on.
questions.explain: Data really does exist there (for example, a value that was just popped), but correctly behaving code never depends on memory beyond the top of the stack.

questions.q: Which of these can be found on the stack?
questions.explain: The stack holds return addresses, locals, sometimes arguments, saved registers, and alloca() space. malloc() allocates from the heap.

questions.q: Why does a function call put a return address on the stack?
choices: So the called function knows where to go back to in the calling function
So the caller can find the callee's local variables
So the OS can relocate the program
So the heap knows where the stack ends
questions.explain: When one function calls another, a return address is pushed so that the callee can get back to the caller when it finishes.

questions.q: Why might a compiler save register values on the stack?
choices: All functions share the same 16 registers and must not overwrite each other's values, and a complex function may need to juggle more values than fit in registers
Registers lose their values after every instruction
The stack is faster to access than registers
To make the stack grow toward higher addresses
questions.explain: Saving registers lets functions share them without clobbering each other's values. It also gives a complex function somewhere to spill values when 16 registers aren't enough.

questions.q: main() calls foo(), which calls bar(). While bar() is running, which function's frame is at the lowest memory address?
choices: All three share a single frame
questions.explain: Each call creates a new frame further toward lower addresses, so bar's frame is at the top of the stack (lowest address) and main's is nearest the bottom. Frames disappear as functions return.

questions.q: Stack diagrams are always drawn with high addresses at the top and the stack growing downward.
questions.explain: Conventions vary. Some people draw the stack growing upward, and 'Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit' draws it horizontally. You need to be able to read the stack in any orientation.

questions.q: In 64-bit mode, by how many bytes does PUSH decrement RSP?
questions.explain: PUSH stores a quadword (8 bytes) and automatically subtracts 8 from RSP. The stack grows toward lower addresses.

questions.q: RAX = 3 and RSP = 0x14FE08 (the value 2 is stored there). After `push rax`, which is true?
choices: RSP = 0x14FE00, and the 8 bytes at 0x14FE00 hold 3
RSP = 0x14FE10, and the 8 bytes at 0x14FE10 hold 3
RSP = 0x14FE08, and the 2 there is overwritten with 3
questions.explain: PUSH subtracts 8 from RSP (0x14FE08 to 0x14FE00) and writes RAX there. RSP then points at the newly pushed 3. RAX itself is unchanged.

questions.q: RAX = 0x5007 and RSP = 0x14FE00 (the value 3 is stored there). After `pop rax`, which is true?
choices: RAX = 3, RSP = 0x14FE00, and the slot is zeroed
questions.explain: POP copies the value at RSP into RAX, overwriting 0x5007, and then adds 8 to RSP. The slot at 0x14FE00 is now undefined.

questions.q: POP zeroes the stack slot it reads from.
questions.explain: Neither the hardware nor compiler-generated code clears it. The old value is still there, but because it is beyond the top of the stack it is considered undefined.

questions.q: Right after a PUSH, RSP points at the value that was just pushed.
questions.explain: RSP always points at the top of the stack, meaning the last value stored. It does not point at the next free slot.

questions.q: RSP = 0x14FE10, RAX = 0xA, RBX = 0xB. You execute `push rax`, `push rbx`, `pop rcx`. What is the result?
questions.explain: Two pushes bring RSP down to 0x14FE00. Because the stack is LIFO, the pop returns the last value pushed (0xB) and RSP goes back up by 8 to 0x14FE08.

questions.q: In 64-bit mode, a function executes 3 pushes and then 1 pop. How many bytes lower is RSP than where it started?
questions.explain: 3 x 8 = 24 bytes down, then 8 back up, for a net 16 bytes lower.

questions.q: In 32-bit mode, by how many bytes does a PUSH decrement ESP?
questions.explain: In 32-bit mode, push and pop move 32-bit values, so ESP changes by 4 instead of 8.

questions.q: In 16-bit mode, push and pop change SP by:
questions.explain: 16-bit mode pushes and pops 16-bit values, so SP moves by 2.

questions.q: In 64-bit mode, which of these can be the operand of POP?
choices: A 64-bit memory location in r/mX form, e.g. [rbx]
questions.explain: POP needs somewhere to store the value, either a 64-bit register or a memory location. You can't pop into a constant.

questions.q: According to Intel's PUSH table, `PUSH r/m32` is valid in 64-bit mode.
questions.explain: The table marks PUSH r/m32 (and PUSH r32) as N.E. (not encodable) in 64-bit mode. PUSH r/m16 and PUSH r/m64 are valid there.

questions.q: In the Hello World disassemblies, whose main had no push/pop pair and instead adjusted RSP with `sub rsp,28h` ... `add rsp,28h`?
choices: None: all three used push rbp / pop rbp
questions.explain: Both GCC (Linux) and clang (macOS) started main with push rbp and ended it with a balanced pop rbp. Visual Studio's version only used sub/add on RSP.

questions.q: In Intel syntax, what does `[rbx]` mean?
choices: Treat rbx's value as a memory address and fetch the value stored there
Use the value in rbx itself
Use the address of the rbx register
Treat rbx as an array of bytes
questions.explain: Square brackets mean dereference, like a pointer: the value pointed to by rbx is used, not rbx itself.

questions.q: `push rbx` and `push [rbx]` push the same value.
questions.explain: push rbx pushes the value in rbx. push [rbx] treats rbx as an address and pushes the 64-bit value stored in memory at that address.

questions.q: What does 'r/mX' stand for?
choices: Any operand the Intel manual writes as r/m8, r/m16, r/m32 or r/m64: either a register or a memory location of that size
Memory operands only, never a register
A register that holds an X coordinate
An immediate value that is X bits wide
questions.explain: An r/mX operand can be as simple as a plain register or as complex as [base + index*scale + displacement].

questions.q: Which values are allowed as the scale in [base + index*scale]?
questions.explain: The scale can only be 1, 2, 4 or 8. No other values are allowed.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid r/mX memory form?
questions.explain: The scale must be 1, 2, 4 or 8, so *3 can't be encoded. The other three are base-only, base+index*scale, and base+index*scale+displacement.

questions.q: In `[rbx+rcx*8+0x20]`, what role does each part play?
choices: rbx = base, rcx = index, 8 = scale, 0x20 = displacement
rbx = index, rcx = base, 8 = displacement, 0x20 = scale
rbx = base, rcx = scale, 8 = index, 0x20 = displacement
rbx = displacement, rcx = index, 8 = scale, 0x20 = base
questions.explain: The general form is [base + index*scale + displacement].

questions.q: rbx = 0x1000 and rcx = 3. What memory address does `[rbx+rcx*8+0x20]` refer to?
questions.explain: 0x1000 + 3*8 (0x18) + 0x20 = 0x1038. The value fetched is whatever is stored at that address.

questions.q: In the base+index*scale+displacement form, how can the displacement be encoded?
choices: At any size up to 64 bits
questions.explain: The displacement is encoded in either 1 byte (0 to 2^8) or 4 bytes (0 to 2^32).

questions.q: The [base + index*scale + displacement] form is especially natural for accessing:
choices: Multi-dimensional arrays and arrays of structs
questions.explain: Base = start of the array, index*scale = element number times element size, displacement = extra offset such as a row or field offset.

questions.q: What does the backtick in 0x00000000`0014FE08 mark?
choices: The split between the two 32-bit halves of a 64-bit number (WinDbg-style notation)
The boundary between an address and the value stored there
questions.explain: The backtick separates the upper and lower 32 bits, which makes it easy to check that a 64-bit number has the right number of digits. WinDbg is probably the only tool that accepts numbers typed this way.

questions.q: A number written as 0x00000001`00003F50 needs more than 32 bits to represent.
questions.explain: A non-zero value to the left of the backtick means the upper 32 bits are in use, so the number is larger than 32 bits.
